title: Lessons in Love
description: Level 42's biggest hit, a slap-bass anthem released a full year before the album it eventually opened.

pops.text: Released on 14 April 1986, this single arrived almost a year before its album, Running in the Family, in March 1987.
Mark King says the tune began as an extra closing tag the band tacked onto live performances of 'Physical Presence.'
It was written by King with Wally Badarou and Rowland 'Boon' Gould — Badarou was the band's unofficial fifth member on synths.
King's bridge is a neat trick: it flips the main chord sequence upside down and runs it back up to the chorus.
This became Level 42's biggest UK hit, reaching No. 3 — still their highest-charting single at home.
It went all the way to No. 1 in Germany, Spain, Finland, South Africa, Switzerland and Denmark.
Director Stuart Orme shot the video with the band performing aboard a cargo ship, using early green-screen for the bright blue sky.
The rush release had a reason: a German artist was about to cover it, so Level 42 had to get their own version out first.
In the US it reached No. 12 in 1987, and it led off a run of five singles from Running in the Family.

title: Valerie
description: Mark Ronson and Amy Winehouse turn a year-old Zutons indie song into a brassy soul-pop smash.

pops.text: This is a cover — Liverpool band The Zutons released the original in 2006 and took it to No. 9 in the UK.
The real Valerie is Valerie Star, a New York celebrity makeup artist who was dating Zutons singer Dave McCabe.
McCabe wrote the song in about 20 minutes in the back of a taxi on his way to his mother's house.
Its lyric pleading with Valerie to come over was rooted in her legal trouble in the US, which kept her from travelling to see him.
Ronson's production is built around the beat from The Jam's 1982 hit 'A Town Called Malice.'
Winehouse first sang it for BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge before it became the third single from Ronson's album Version.
It peaked at No. 2 in the UK and spent 19 straight weeks inside the Top 20.
Director Robert Hales' video works around Winehouse's absence: Ronson pulls a lookalike fan from the audience to mime the song on stage.
It was nominated for British Single of the Year at the 2008 BRIT Awards, and later spent four weeks at No. 1 in the Netherlands.

title: Get Lucky
artist: Daft Punk featuring Pharrell Williams and Nile Rodgers
description: Daft Punk ditch samples for live disco, teaming with Pharrell Williams and Chic's Nile Rodgers — note: this is the official audio, as no full official music video was made.

pops.text: Released 19 April 2013 as the lead single from Random Access Memories, Daft Punk's first album in eight years.
Daft Punk first met Nile Rodgers back in 1997, at a New York listening party for their debut album Homework.
Rodgers recorded at Electric Lady Studios — the same studio where Chic's first single was made, in the neighbourhood where he grew up.
Hearing the demo, Rodgers asked for everything muted except the drums, then built his signature choppy guitar part over the bare groove.
His part was so central that Daft Punk had bassist Nathan East re-record the bass line afterwards to fit Rodgers' guitar.
The whole song loops just four chords at 116 BPM, with Pharrell's lead vocal and Daft Punk's vocoder spanning three octaves.
Daft Punk were perfectionists about Pharrell's vocals, making him repeat phrases again and again across many takes.
It hit No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 for five straight weeks — Daft Punk's first-ever US Top 10 hit.
It won Record of the Year and Best Pop Duo/Group Performance at the Grammys, where Stevie Wonder joined them live on stage.

title: Pumped Up Kicks
description: A sunny, whistling indie-pop hit with a deliberately dark lyric, written in five hours as a demo that was never re-recorded.

pops.text: Mark Foster wrote this in 2009 while working as a commercial jingle writer at Mophonics in Venice, California.
He wrote and recorded it in about five hours, playing every instrument himself in Logic Pro.
What you're hearing is the demo — Foster never re-recorded it, and that demo became the released single.
Foster said he wrote it after reading about rising teenage mental illness, trying to get inside an isolated teenager's head.
The band posted it as a free download in early 2010, and a Nylon magazine campaign plus a German music blog helped it spread.
Released as their debut single in September 2010, it later landed on the band's debut album Torches in 2011.
It topped Billboard's Alternative Songs chart in June 2011 before crossing over to pop radio.
It then sat at No. 3 on the Hot 100 for eight consecutive weeks, stuck behind Adele and Maroon 5's 'Moves Like Jagger.'
It earned a Grammy nomination for Best Pop Duo/Group Performance, and was Spotify's most-streamed song of 2011.

title: It's My Life
description: No Doubt revive Talk Talk's 1984 synth-pop gem as the lone new track on their first greatest-hits album.

pops.text: This started life in 1984 as the title track of Talk Talk's second album, written by Mark Hollis and Tim Friese-Greene.
It was the only brand-new song on No Doubt's first hits collection, The Singles 1992-2003.
The band listened to hundreds of possible covers and narrowed the final choice down to this and INXS's 'Don't Change.'
With Gwen Stefani heading toward a solo album, a cover spared the band writing a new song — rehearsing this one with producer Nellee Hooper sealed the deal.
Hooper, known for work with Björk and Massive Attack, produced the track, and programmer Jacques Lu Cont later gave it his Thin White Duke remix.
The gamble paid off on the charts: No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100, where it hung around for 28 weeks.
Director David LaChapelle filmed the 1930s-style video at Los Angeles's Ambassador Hotel, with Stefani styled like Jean Harlow as a black widow on trial.
Her three victims are her own bandmates — one poisoned at dinner, one run down by car, and one electrocuted by a hairdryer dropped in the bath.
The video won Best Group Video and Best Pop Video at the 2004 MTV VMAs, and the song earned a Grammy nomination for Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group.

title: Hip to Be Square
description: Huey Lewis and the News celebrate clean living and conformity in this horn-driven hit from the chart-topping Fore!

pops.text: Band members Bill Gibson, Sean Hopper and Huey Lewis wrote this together, and it came out in October 1986 as the second single from Fore!
Fore! itself hit No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and spun off five Top 10 singles.
Listen for the backing vocals: San Francisco 49ers Joe Montana, Ronnie Lott, Dwight Clark and Riki Ellison sing the 'here, there and everywhere' lines.
The very last 'hip to be square' before the fade is Dwight Clark — quarterback Joe Montana himself confirmed Dwight was the singer of the group.
The single reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped Billboard's Album Rock Tracks chart.
Directors Godley & Creme shot the video on a sound stage using medical cameras to get extreme close-ups of the band and their instruments.
That offbeat video earned a nomination for Most Experimental Video at the 1987 MTV Video Music Awards.
Patrick Bateman praises the song at length in the novel American Psycho, then repeats the lecture in the film right before the infamous axe scene.
Sesame Street gave it a kid-friendly twist as 'Hip to Be a Square,' a cartoon segment all about shapes.

title: My Doorbell
description: Jack White swaps guitar for pounding piano on this Motown-flavoured stomp from Get Behind Me Satan.

pops.text: Released in July 2005 as the second single from Get Behind Me Satan, this one trades Jack White's fuzz guitar for pounding piano.
The album was recorded at Jack's Detroit home, with the piano set up in the foyer and Meg's drums perched on the second-floor stair landing.
For all its loose, party feel, the song itself was recorded in just two takes.
Critics heard a strong Motown flavour in the groove, and Jack has credited Meg with giving the track its distinctive beat.
Jack told Rolling Stone he loves singing this song but hates playing it, calling the piano part a harsh rhythm.
It climbed to No. 10 on the UK Singles Chart, No. 1 on the UK Indie chart, and No. 13 on US alternative airplay.
The black-and-white video, directed by the Malloys, puts Jack and Meg in front of a crowd of children at Hollywood's Magic Castle, filmed over two days in July 2005.
The song earned a 2006 Grammy nomination for Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals, while its parent album won Best Alternative Music Album.
Spot the family help: Jack's brother Eddie Gillis chips in on tambourine and shakers, and the track even makes room for electric bass.

title: Paradise by the Dashboard Light
description: Jim Steinman's eight-minute teenage rock opera, duetted by Meat Loaf and Ellen Foley, baseball commentary and all.

pops.text: Songwriter Jim Steinman built this as a mini rock opera for Bat Out of Hell, produced by Todd Rundgren and released in 1977.
The album version runs eight and a half minutes in three parts — Paradise, Let It Sleep on It, and Praying for the End of Time — though Meat Loaf said Steinman's original idea ran 27 minutes.
Yankees announcer Phil Rizzuto recorded his baseball play-by-play in 1976 at New York's Hit Factory, using phrases written to sound like his real calls.
Two members of Bruce Springsteen's E Street Band play on the album sessions: pianist Roy Bittan and drummer Max Weinberg.
The voice sparring with Meat Loaf on the record is Ellen Foley — but the woman in the video is Karla DeVito, lip-syncing Foley's vocal on tour and on screen.
Meat Loaf talked his label into $30,000 to film live-on-a-soundstage performances of three Bat Out of Hell songs, this one included.
As a US single it only reached No. 39 on the Billboard Hot 100, yet FM radio turned it into an inescapable classic-rock staple.
In the Netherlands it did far better, hitting No. 1 and becoming Meat Loaf's biggest hit there ever.
The promo film became a staple of MTV's early years and was screened before midnight showings of The Rocky Horror Picture Show.

title: True
description: Spandau Ballet's silky blue-eyed soul ballad, written by Gary Kemp as a tribute to Marvin Gaye and a crush he never confessed out loud.

pops.text: Gary Kemp wrote this one at his parents' house, where he was still living at the time.
That line about listening to Marvin all night long? A direct salute to Marvin Gaye, Kemp's soul hero.
Kemp was quietly smitten with Altered Images singer Clare Grogan — this song was his way of saying it without saying it.
Some lyric phrases were borrowed from Nabokov's Lolita — a copy Grogan herself had given Kemp.
Kemp built the song around bandmate Steve Norman's new love: the saxophone. That smooth sax became its signature.
The band ditched their New Romantic look for sharp suits to match this new soul direction.
It spent four weeks at No. 1 in the UK — still the band's only British chart-topper.
In America it hit No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped the Adult Contemporary chart.
P.M. Dawn sampled it for their 1991 No. 1 'Set Adrift on Memory Bliss,' sending True back to the top by proxy.

title: Break My Stride
description: Matthew Wilder's unstoppable bounce-back anthem — official VEVO audio (no official music video upload exists on his channel), born from frustration with his own record label.

pops.text: Note: this is the official VEVO audio upload — Wilder's official channel offers no original music video for this song.
Wilder wrote this while stuck at Arista Records, frustrated that things were not going his way.
He later said the song poured out of him in about 30 minutes, at the peak of that frustration.
Broke and unconvinced by his label, Wilder paid for the recording himself, in the early hours at a producer's studio.
Arista boss Clive Davis heard it and passed — the label let Wilder go.
Because Arista had never paid for the sessions, Wilder owned the tapes and could shop them elsewhere. Lucky break!
New label Private-I released it, and the rejected song climbed to No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100.
It also hit No. 4 in the UK and No. 2 on the Cash Box chart — not bad for a song deemed not a hit.
In 2020 it exploded on TikTok as a lyric-texting prank, and Wilder answered with an official lyric video built from text messages.

title: I Think We're Alone Now
description: Teen star Tiffany turned a 1967 Tommy James hit into a mall-tour phenomenon and a transatlantic No. 1.

pops.text: This song was already a hit once: Tommy James and the Shondells took it to No. 4 back in 1967.
Songwriter Ritchie Cordell wrote it in the 1960s — Tiffany's producer George Tobin had always loved it.
Tiffany herself was not keen at first — she worried the dancey track would not show off her singing.
Then she played it for friends doing homework, they all started dancing, and she changed her mind.
Tobin promoted her with a shopping-mall tour, singing for free to shoppers across America in 1987.
The video is basically that mall tour on film — shot in Utah shopping malls, with extra footage in Birmingham, England.
It spent two weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a huge run for a singer still in her mid-teens.
In the UK it held No. 1 for three weeks — and Tiffany had only just turned 16.
It was knocked off the US top spot by Billy Idol's 'Mony Mony' — incredibly, another Tommy James cover. Two in a row!

title: We Belong
description: Pat Benatar softened her rock edge for this soaring power ballad from Tropico, written in about 90 minutes by Lowen & Navarro.

pops.text: Benatar did not write this one — it came from songwriting duo Eric Lowen and Dan Navarro.
The pair reportedly put the song together in about 90 minutes, sparked by Navarro lamenting an old flame.
Dan Navarro is the first cousin of Jane's Addiction guitarist Dave Navarro. Rock runs in the family!
This was the lead single from Tropico, an album where Benatar deliberately leaned into a softer, more melodic sound.
Hear the ending swell? A children's choir joins in to lift the final chorus.
Fun production quirk: the video uses the 7-inch version, which has extra vocals in the intro you won't hear on the album cut.
It peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 — exactly matching 'Love Is a Battlefield.'
In Britain it reached No. 22, becoming Benatar's first UK Top 40 hit.
The song earned Benatar a Grammy nomination for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance, and later turned up in Deadpool 2.

title: Carry On Wayward Son
description: Kansas's breakthrough prog-rock anthem — this is the official VEVO video upload (a period performance video, not a modern concept clip), for a song that nearly never made the album.

pops.text: No concept music video existed in 1976 — this official VEVO upload is a period performance video. That a cappella opening still stops you cold.
Writer Kerry Livgren brought this in on the very last day of rehearsals, as the band was packing to leave Topeka to record.
The others groaned at learning one more song — then heard it and knew instantly it had to go on the album.
Livgren carried the album's writing load because co-writer Steve Walsh had hit a bout of writer's block.
Livgren called the song autobiographical — a self-pep talk from his own spiritual searching.
It opens the album Leftoverture, recorded at Studio in the Country in Louisiana with producer Jeff Glixman.
At nearly six minutes on the album, nobody expected a hit — the single was trimmed to about 3:26 for radio.
It became Kansas's first Top 40 hit, peaking at No. 11 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1977.
Decades later, TV's Supernatural adopted it for nearly every season finale recap — 'the road so far' — giving it a whole second life.

description: Australian trio PNAU stitch four Elton John classics into a shimmering dance track sung by Elton and Dua Lipa.

pops.text: Four Elton songs in one! PNAU mash up Rocket Man (1972), Where's the Shoorah? (1976), Kiss the Bride (1983) and Sacrifice (1989) into a single track.
This pairing started as a friendship in November 2020, when Elton appeared on Dua's Studio 2054 livestream and she later sang at his AIDS Foundation Oscars party.
PNAU had done this trick before: their 2012 Elton remix album Good Morning to the Night reworked his catalogue and went to No. 1 in the UK.
Released 13 August 2021, this was the lead single from The Lockdown Sessions, an album Elton recorded over 18 months during the pandemic, much of it remotely.
Listen to who sings what: Dua takes the Rocket Man chorus and Kiss the Bride, Elton sings Sacrifice, and Where's the Shoorah? sneaks in as the coda at the end.
No live shoot was possible in lockdown, so Hamburg animator Raman Djafari directed this video, sending cartoon Elton and Dua dancing through a psychedelic galaxy.
Slow burner: it entered the UK chart at No. 33, then climbed to No. 1 in its ninth week — Elton's eighth UK No. 1 and his first since 2005, and Dua's third.
That UK No. 1 made Elton the first solo artist to score a UK top 10 single in six different decades. The song also topped charts in Australia for 10 weeks and peaked at No. 7 in the US.
In November 2022 Dua joined Elton live at Dodger Stadium for his final North American show, streamed on Disney+ — and the song won Collaboration of the Year at the American Music Awards.

title: Cold Heart

description: Dua Lipa's glittering disco lead single from Barbie the Album, built for the film's big choreographed dance scene.

pops.text: The whole Barbie soundtrack started with a one-word text to producer Mark Ronson from music supervisor George Drakoulias: 'Barbie?'
Director Greta Gerwig asked for disco, sending Ronson a playlist inspired by the Bee Gees and Saturday Night Fever for the film's big dance sequence.

Ronson and Andrew Wyatt's early backing track was called 'Tastes Like Barbie' — Gerwig loved it so much she said she played it 100 times on her way to set, and the cast rehearsed to it before it had lyrics.
Ronson slid into Dua's Instagram DMs because the track sounded like her album Future Nostalgia. She flew to New York and wrote the lyrics with Caroline Ailin in about a week.

Dua wrote it like a film score, syncing lines to the on-screen choreography — even tweaking parts to match Margot Robbie's hand movements. Her brief to herself: dance-crying, flawless on the outside, heartbroken underneath.
That sparkle is real strings — cello, violin and viola over the synths, with the Picard Brothers helping on the string arrangement, Wyatt on bass and synth, and Ronson on guitar and Rhodes piano.
Video secrets: Dua dances atop a giant Barbie heel in pieces from La Vacanza, her collection with Donatella Versace, intercut with Margot Robbie, Issa Rae and Emma Mackey dancing in the film.

When that giant disco ball crashes to the floor, it's symbolic — Ronson said it marks Dua moving away from the Future Nostalgia dance sound. Greta Gerwig herself cameos at the end, asking what happened to it.

Released 25 May 2023 as the soundtrack's lead single, it became Dua's fourth UK No. 1 and reached No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 — then earned Grammy nominations for Song of the Year and Best Song Written for Visual Media.

title: Dance The Night
